name: Education & Research AI
intro:
Education and research AI covers tools built specifically for academic use, where the buyer is a school, university, or student and the product has to answer to FERPA, COPPA, or an honor code, not just general-purpose data protection. That framing is the boundary: this category excludes general writing or research assistants that happen to get used by students, and it excludes AI features inside learning management systems that are not sold as a distinct product. What sits inside it are four tools built around that academic relationship: Khanmigo, Khan Academy's tutoring assistant, Grammarly for Education, Turnitin's AI detection product, and CheggMate, Chegg's study assistant.

A buyer here is choosing between fundamentally different roles for AI in the classroom. Khanmigo positions AI as a Socratic tutor that guides students toward answers, Grammarly for Education positions it as institutional writing support with governance controls, Turnitin positions it as a policing layer that flags AI-generated submissions, and CheggMate positions it as homework help, the same category of use Turnitin exists to catch.

That tension defined the last year. Turnitin's AI detector remains contested on accuracy. Curtin University announced in 2026 that it would disable the tool campus-wide, joining a broader wave of institutions questioning false-positive rates. Meanwhile Chegg's own business, built on the homework-help model CheggMate extends, collapsed under AI competition: the company cut 45 percent of its workforce in October 2025 and its stock has lost roughly 99 percent of its value since ChatGPT's launch, citing students turning directly to free AI tools instead of paying for Chegg.

Khanmigo is the clearest reference point for tutoring done well, and Turnitin remains the reference for detection, despite its accuracy problems, because no credible academic-integrity alternative has displaced it.

Twenty more tools were added on 2026-10-02 from the research behind The AI Ready School, Volume X of The Operating Discipline for AI Library, where each was checked for the questions a school has to answer before students touch it: what the AI actually does, the youngest age a student may use it, which privacy agreement covers it, and what it costs. They fall into four groups. Teacher platforms and assistants: MagicSchool, ChatGPT for Teachers, Gemini for Education, Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat and Google's meeting notes. Creative and learning tools: Canva and Adobe Express for Education, Duolingo for Schools, Google Teachable Machine, iNaturalist and GitHub Copilot for students. Accessibility and language: Microsoft Immersive Reader, live captions, Translator and Seeing AI, Be My Eyes, Read&Write, Proloquo2Go and TalkingPoints for families. And one research system, Stanford's Tutor CoPilot, which coaches human tutors rather than replacing them. Age limits differ sharply across them, from no login at all to 18 and over, so each entry states its own.

The rest of the products that research turned up are listed here too, because schools use them, but read their entries with care. Many are not AI products at all (Google Docs and Sheets, Desmos, GeoGebra, robotics kits, music and data tools), and each entry says so. Others were found in the research but could not be confirmed from an official source for student age, privacy terms or price, and their entries open with "not independently verified". Treat those as a starting point for a district's own review, not as a finding. Student monitoring products such as Gaggle, GoGuardian Beacon and Bark carry the book's caution that there is no evidence monitoring prevents harm.

tools.name: Adobe Express for Education
tools.note: AI: Firefly generative AI. Who: K-12 teachers and students. Student age: K-12 students by teacher invite or district provisioning. Privacy: Education privacy controls; no ads or paywalls in the K-12 version. Price: Free for K-12 schools and districts.
tools.source: The AI Ready School (Volume X), research verified 2026-09-29, chapters 10

tools.name: Amira Learning
tools.note: Found in the research for The AI Ready School; not independently verified. AI: Speech recognition tutoring in English and Spanish. Use: AI reading tutor, fluency assessment, dyslexia screening. Who: Students PreK to 8, teachers. Student age: PreK to 8 students rostered by the district; vendor states COPPA compliance. Privacy: District data privacy agreements (signed example in SDPC registry, Scottsdale USD, 2024); vendor states student data is not sent to public AI models. In June 2026 a Portland board member questioned contract data fields such as place of birth and migrant status, and New Mexico let districts opt out of voice recording. Price: Screener $4.99 per student; full suite $20 per student (California state filing, 2024); some states fund free access. Caution: Vendor-cited research; see Chapter 6 evidence notes.
tools.source: The AI Ready School (Volume X) research, chapters 5,6

tools.name: Amplify mCLASS
tools.note: Verified in the research for The AI Ready School. AI: Automatic scoring; no speech recognition. Use: DIBELS 8 early literacy screening. Who: Teachers, students K to 6. Student age: School license. Privacy: Signed Texas student data privacy agreement (TX-NDPA) with Midway ISD, 2025, in the SDPC registry. Price: $9 per student for one year or $7 multi-year (California filing); Lectura add-on $5; DIBELS Data System alternative $1 per student plus $200 setup.

reading.body:
Education AI tools in the US market split between student assistance, writing support, tutoring, and integrity monitoring, all handling student data subject to FERPA and COPPA oversight.

The four dominant tools serve opposing functions within the same institutions. CheggMate and Khanmigo help students learn or complete work. Grammarly for Education supports writing at scale. Turnitin detects AI-generated content to enforce academic integrity. Institutions must now run assistance and detection in parallel, creating a technical and policy problem: the same student data flows through tools meant to help and tools meant to catch, each with different compliance obligations and false-positive risks.

This fragmentation reflects a deeper tension. AI capability in education creates immediate demand from students but generates institutional liability around honor codes and data handling. Turnitin's AI detection tool introduces its own hazard: flagging human work as machine-generated, with stakes that affect student records. None of these tools' notes indicate shared infrastructure or standardized data handling, suggesting each operates independently despite overlapping access to FERPA-protected information.

The data does not cover which tools dominate by adoption, how often detection errors occur, or whether institutions have established policies for when assistance and detection conflict. It also does not address whether these tools require additional compute or power to operate, their resource footprint, or consolidation trends among vendors.
